rich_summary: Yudhishthira instructs Sanjaya to deliver a carefully balanced message to the Kuru court. While acknowledging Dhritarashtra’s past support, he insists that the Pandavas deserve their rightful share of the kingdom. Yudhishthira emphasizes restraint: despite grave insults—especially Draupadi’s humiliation and their exile—the Pandavas have endured in order to avoid the destruction of the Kuru family. He proposes peace on remarkably modest terms, asking even for just five villages to avert war. Sanjaya then travels to Hastinapura and reports to Dhritarashtra, describing Yudhishthira as virtuous, restrained, and guided by righteousness rather than greed. He warns the blind king that destiny and the consequences of his own wrongful choices threaten disaster, subtly urging him to reconsider before conflict becomes inevitable.

highlight_spans.why: Yudhishthira opens with a philosophical reflection on destiny and divine control, setting the moral tone of the chapter.
The statement that the Creator gives wisdom or childishness highlights the theme of divine will guiding human affairs.
Yudhishthira’s respectful instructions to greet Dhritarashtra emphasize humility despite injustice.
The appeal that the kingdom should not belong to one person underscores the central political argument for shared rule.
References to Draupadi’s humiliation and the Pandavas’ restraint convey the emotional weight behind their demand for justice.

top_scenes.scene_text: Yudhishthira calmly addressing Sanjaya among the assembled Pandavas, instructing him to carry a plea for peace and justice to the Kuru court.
Sanjaya arriving at the gates of the palace in Hastinapura at night, respectfully announcing himself to the gatekeeper with an urgent message from the Pandavas.
Sanjaya standing before the blind king Dhritarashtra in the royal hall, delivering Yudhishthira’s message while courtiers watch tensely.
